chunks: "Reflow is how surface-mount parts get soldered. Solder paste, which is tiny solder balls in flux, is printed on the pads and parts are placed on it.
The whole board then rides a conveyor through an oven that follows a temperature profile, which melts the paste so the solder wets the pads and leads, and then cools it so the joints freeze.
The profile has four phases. Preheat ramps the board gently, around one to three degrees per second, so nothing cracks from thermal shock.
The soak holds it around 150 to 180 degrees Celsius for a minute or so to let temperature even out across the board and activate the flux, which strips oxide.

Then the reflow zone ramps above the solder's melting point, about 217 degrees Celsius for common lead-free alloys, to a peak of roughly 240 to 250 degrees Celsius, and holds above melting for something like 45 to 90 seconds so the solder wets and flows.
Finally controlled cooling freezes the joints into a fine grain structure.
The tricky bit is the window: the solder needs to be hot enough to wet but the parts have a maximum temperature, so you profile real boards with thermocouples and adjust the oven zones.
A bad profile gives cold joints, voids, solder balls or tombstoned parts."
